episode_title: 138:- Entrepreneur Like a Mother: Beth Mazza on Business Growth and Motherhood

real_qa.q: What is the core premise of Entrepreneur Like a Mother and why did Beth Mazza write it?
real_qa.r: The book is mission-based around helping mothers realize they can build successful businesses. Beth and her co-author Victoria, together mothers of nine children, built businesses that gave them financial freedom and retired early, but lasted only two weeks in retirement. They felt compelled to share their story because they heard so many mothers saying they should wait or do a side hustle instead, and they wanted to show mothers: no, girl, you got this.
real_qa.requete: Entrepreneur Like a Mother book Beth Mazza

real_qa.q: What is the one fallacy that holds mothers back from becoming entrepreneurs?
real_qa.r: The fallacy is that mothers are safer in corporate and can be more flexible there, but the math says otherwise. Corporations lay off 10% of their workforce every year, so after 10 years employees are likely to be ditched. Women suffer further as they move up, often being underpaid, unhappy, and the only one in the room who looks like them or is a mother. Starting with the understanding that this fallacy is false opens your mind to becoming a mom and an entrepreneur.
real_qa.requete: Why corporate is not safe for mothers entrepreneurs

real_qa.q: What does Beth Mazza say mothers actually need to succeed in business?
real_qa.r: Mothers need two core things: a kitchen cabinet of cheerleaders and connectors who help you network and learn without attending 97 events, and a compensator—someone in your network who can educate you quickly on industries or client types you lack experience in. Beyond that, mothers need to give themselves grace: focus on one hard thing per day for your business rather than trying to do ten, string together 30 hard things over time, and accept that you will not be perfect every day.
real_qa.requete: What do mothers need to build a successful business

real_qa.q: How does Beth Mazza recommend mothers approach scaling their business?
real_qa.r: The key is unscaling through delegation: identify the three things only you can do in your business where nobody will do it as well, and let 70% of everything else go. Beth categorizes work into three buckets—only you can do it, someone else can do it with oversight needed, and someone else can do it and it doesn't matter. When Beth's partner Victoria was doing invoices at 3 a.m. at $7-8 million revenue, they hired a part-time CFO to offload everything except core work, which freed Victoria from PTSD-inducing tasks and accelerated their growth.
real_qa.requete: How to scale business by delegating as a mother entrepreneur

real_qa.q: What is the financial framework Beth Mazza uses to determine when to make first hires?
real_qa.r: Create aspirational financials: calculate what your salary would need to be to replace your corporate income, then determine at what percentage of that target you could afford both personal and professional hires. Frame the first hire as a low-risk 60-90 day trial by dividing the annual salary by the number of days, not as a full $100,000 investment. Be transparent with new hires that the first 90 days are a trial period where both parties assess fit, and remember that you cannot scale or gain financial freedom without hires—95% of companies cannot replace a corporate salary without building a team.
real_qa.requete: When should mothers hire first employee for their business

guest.bio_context: Beth Mazza is a mother of four and three-time entrepreneur who has exited two million-dollar companies. She co-authored the book Entrepreneur Like a Mother with her business partner Victoria, together raising nine children. The book launched in September and hit the USA Today bestseller list within two weeks. She and her co-author retired early after building businesses that provided financial freedom, then launched The Female Maverick to help other mothers start and scale their own enterprises.
